summary: Verse is Epic Games' programming language for gameplay, the one Unreal Editor for Fortnite runs and the one Epic says its future engine will use. It is a subject on this map because of what it says about code, not about content: every function declares in its own signature what it may do — read memory, write it, fail, suspend, or run on the client ahead of the server — and the compiler enforces that declaration; state changed inside a failing branch is rolled back automatically; concurrency is in the language itself, with expressions that run several things at once, race them, or let one outlive its scope; and every published module has a permanent address that nobody else may ever claim. The row that should interest a standards group most is versioning: compatibility here is not a convention but a rule checked when code is published — a public definition can never be removed, renamed or changed in kind, and effects may only ever be dropped, never added — which is enforcement rather than policy, and is the one mechanism here a working group could copy rather than merely record. Everything about scenes, geometry, avatars, audio, positioning and devices is out of scope: this is a language, and its reference specifies none of it. Two traps. First, portability: the language reference is published under a public-domain dedication and is genuinely open to read, but the only implementation is a virtual machine held in a repository Epic has not published, so Verse code cannot be run, checked or replayed anywhere except inside Epic's own service — the 594 executable tests that ship with the reference cannot be run without Epic's binaries. Second, the reference documents the head of a development branch, so several things it describes in full — client prediction, reactive live variables, serialisation of saved data — are marked in the text itself as not yet released, and a reader who scores from the prose alone will credit Verse with features nobody can use today.

coverage.note: The language reference specifies no renderer at all: its nineteen chapters cover expressions, types, effects, concurrency, modules and persistence, and nothing about drawing. There is no rasterizer, render graph or pass structure anywhere in the reference.

coverage.note: Verse gives determinism at the language level and says nothing about simulation across machines. Functions marked pure are deterministic by the compiler's rule, the wall clock is frozen inside a transaction so a retry cannot see a different time, and module initialisation is deterministic by construction. None of that is a promise that two machines running the same world reach the same state; the reference never makes that promise.

sources.title: Book of Verse, Effects, pure computation
sources.quote: The `<computes>` specifier marks pure functions — those that neither read nor write mutable state. These functions are deterministic: given the same inputs, they always produce the same outputs.

sources.title: Book of Verse, Concurrency, GetSecondsSinceEpoch
sources.quote: Within a single transaction, `GetSecondsSinceEpoch()` returns the **same value** every time it is called. This ensures deterministic behavior and prevents time-related race conditions

coverage.note: This is the whole of the subject. Verse is a statically checked, multi-paradigm language with everything-is-an-expression semantics, failure as first-class control flow, a compiler-enforced effect system, structured concurrency and a type system that catches errors before the code runs.

sources.title: Book of Verse, Overview
sources.quote: Verse is a multi-paradigm programming language developed by Epic Games for creating gameplay in Unreal Editor for Fortnite and building experiences in the metaverse.

sources.title: Book of Verse, Types
sources.quote: The type system combines static verification with practical flexibility, catching errors at compile time while still allowing sophisticated patterns of code reuse and abstraction.

coverage.note: Verse expresses interactivity as compiled code held in modules, not as declarative data carried inside an asset, and the only implementation is a virtual machine that lives in a repository Epic has not published — the documentation's own build instructions require access to it. So a behaviour written in Verse cannot be read, checked or replayed by any other runtime, which is exactly what a portable behaviour graph is for.

coverage.note: Safety for untrusted code is a stated design aim and the machinery for it is real and compiler-enforced: an effect system in six families that says what a function may do, access specifiers and named scopes that say who may call it, and no way to launder an effect through an intermediate function. What is missing is the other half of the definition — the reference sets no limit on memory, time or calls, and the divergence family that would prove termination is described as still in planning.

sources.title: Book of Verse, Overview, design aims
sources.quote: **Safe enough** for untrusted code to run in a shared environment, with strong sandboxing and effect tracking.

sources.title: Book of Verse, Effects, propagation
sources.quote: This propagation ensures that effects can't be hidden or laundered through intermediate functions — the true nature of an operation is always visible at every level of the call stack.

sources.title: Book of Verse, Effects, Divergence effects
sources.quote: Currently in planning, the divergence family will track whether functions are guaranteed to terminate.

coverage.note: A language written for untrusted guest code in a shared simulation is exactly the kind of thing that should bound memory, time and calls, and this one does not. The reference states no budget of any kind. The nearest thing is a termination guarantee marked as still in planning, and it proves a function finishes, not that it stays inside a limit.

sources.title: Book of Verse, Effects, Divergence effects
sources.quote: Currently in planning, the divergence family will track whether functions are guaranteed to terminate. The `<converges>` specifier marks functions that provably complete in finite time, while functions without it might run forever.

sources.title: Book of Verse, Overview, design aims

coverage.note: Persistence in Verse is per person, not per world. A module-scoped map keyed by player, holding any type marked persistable, is saved and is loaded again automatically when that player next arrives. There is no world-scoped store: nothing in the reference persists the state of a place, only what each participant carried.

sources.title: Book of Verse, Persistable Types
sources.quote: Persistable data is stored using module-scoped `weak_map(player, t)` variables, where `t` is any persistable type. When a player joins a game, their previously saved data is automatically loaded into all module-scoped variables of type `weak_map(player, t)`.

coverage.note: The language supplies the store an inventory is built on and no item model at all, and what it stores cannot travel. A persistable class is frozen on publication — final, no superclass, no variable fields, no generics — and a persistable struct cannot be modified after the island is published, so the schema is welded to the place that published it. The serialisation that would let the data out is documented as not yet released.

coverage.note: Verse solves the same problem the other way round. Code is referred to by a permanent path that no one else may ever claim, so the name is the stable handle; there is no hash-based reference anywhere in the reference, and nothing content-addressed to check a payload against.

sources.title: Book of Verse, Modules, Paths
sources.quote: Once a module is published at a particular path, that path belongs to it forever. No other module can ever claim the same path, ensuring that dependencies always resolve to the correct code.

coverage.note: The reference does define a unit of shipped code — a folder is a module, every file in it shares one namespace, and a package sits at the root of a path — and it defines the permanent address that unit is published at. It defines no file format, no manifest and no dependency declaration, and it names no publication route other than Epic's own, so there is nothing a second implementation could package or unpack.

coverage.note: This is the strongest row in the subject and the one a standards audience should read first. Compatibility is not advice, it is a checked rule enforced when code is published: a public definition can never be removed, renamed or changed in kind, a closed set of named values can never gain a member, effects may only ever be dropped and never added, and a breaking edit is refused at publication rather than discovered later. Deprecation is staged, warning first and failing only when an author moves to a new language version.

sources.title: Book of Verse, Code Evolution, enforcement
sources.quote: Verse actively prevents developers from publishing updates that would violate compatibility guarantees, turning what might be runtime failures in other systems into publication-time errors that must be resolved before code can be deployed.

sources.title: Book of Verse, Code Evolution, catalogue
sources.quote: **Cannot remove public definitions.** Once a public variable, function, class, or other definition is published, it must remain available.

sources.title: Book of Verse, Code Evolution, effects
sources.quote: Future versions of the function can have fewer effects—evolving from `<reads>` to `<computes>`—but never more.

coverage.note: Half of a conformance suite is public and the other half is not. The reference repository ships 594 executable test files and a runner for them, which is a real corpus of expected behaviour; but the runner needs Epic's own virtual machine binaries, and the documentation's build instructions say those come from a repository that is not published. So nobody outside Epic can run the tests, and there is no statement anywhere of what passing them would prove.

coverage.note: Verse's Scene Graph defines entity nesting with GetParent and AddEntities, behaviour attachment through components (AddComponents, GetComponent), and bidirectional event propagation: SendUp propagates toward the root, SendDown flows through children, and consuming the event halts propagation. This is a containment protocol: it defines how a contained thing talks to its container and vice versa, and where a message stops.

sources.title: Verse API reference, scenegraph entity class
sources.quote: SendUp will be invoked on this entity's parent. Consuming the event at any point will halt propagation.

coverage.note: Verse persistence is per-player, not per-world. State lives in module-scoped weak_map(player, t) variables that load when a player joins. The documentation does not address writing persisted state with no player present, and structs cannot be modified after island publication. World-keyed durable state with unattended external mutation has no expression in the documented model.
